name: Milk Teeth and Titanium: A Book for Growing Bodies
creator: Priya Solano-Achebe
description: A beloved illustrated children's book explaining augmentation, geneware, and BCI to children ages 4-8 through the story of Nneka, a girl whose family members each have different kinds of chrome and modifications. The physical edition features thermochromic ink illustrations that change when touched, while the neural-feed version delivers gentle haptic sensations timed to the story. It normalizes the full spectrum of bodily choices — from unaugmented to heavily chromed — without hierarchy.
medium: physical hardcover (premium edition) and neural-feed children's channel
cultural_impact: Assigned reading in most Tier 2-4 municipal schools, the book has shaped a generation's earliest understanding of bodily autonomy and modification as normal, personal, and beautiful. It is frequently cited by augmentation-rights advocates as foundational to shifting cultural attitudes.
controversy: The Clearskin and Flatskin movements have repeatedly attempted to have the book pulled from school curricula, calling it corporate-funded pro-augmentation propaganda. HelixCorp's children's imprint did partially fund its production, which critics note is never disclosed in the text.
story_hooks: A Shelf community has bootleg physical copies with hand-drawn additions that tell a darker version of Nneka's story — one where her chrome is repo'd when her family can't make payments.
The original manuscript, with illustrations that were cut for being 'too graphic' about surgical augmentation, surfaces at a gray-market auction.
A Tier 5 child who has never encountered the book becomes obsessed with it as a window into lives completely unlike their own.
